articles.title_orig: ASUS announces ROG XG Station 3 with Thunderbolt 5 and RTX 5090 BTF support
articles.title_zh: ASUS announces ROG XG Station 3 with Thunderbolt 5 and RTX 5090 BTF support
articles.content_orig:
ASUS has officially announced the ROG XG Station 3 , an external graphics card dock that connects to a laptop over Thunderbolt 5 and can hold desktop cards up to the GeForce RTX 5090. Here is what was announced, what it can and can't do, and whether it makes more sense than a dedicated gaming PC.
According to the official ASUS press release dated November 3, 2026, the XG Station 3 is an open-frame dock that holds a full desktop graphics card and links it to a laptop with a single Thunderbolt 5 cable. ASUS lists support for the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 50 Series, RTX PRO 6000 Series, AMD Radeon RX 9000 Series and Intel Arc Series.
VideoCardz notes that ASUS first demonstrated the dock at Computex 2025 and showed it again in May, so this announcement mainly adds connectivity and compatibility details. TechPowerUp and Windows Report also covered the launch. Since this is ASUS's own announcement, the details below come straight from the company.
Yes, on paper. The dock has an integrated GC-HPWR slot for ASUS BTF 2.5 graphics cards, and ASUS names the ROG Astral GeForce RTX 5090 BTF Edition and the TUF Gaming GeForce RTX 5080 BTF OC Edition as examples. BTF cards draw power through that slot, so no PCIe power cable is visible. Standard graphics cards also work, using regular PCIe power cables.
There are two practical limits. First, the dock does not include a power supply: VideoCardz reports that ASUS requires you to install your own SFX or SFX-L PSU with enough capacity for your card. Second, the card has to fit, and the maximum supported size is 361 × 139.3 × 93.9 mm.
ASUS quotes up to 80 Gbps of bidirectional bandwidth, twice that of Thunderbolt 4, and up to 120 Gbps with Thunderbolt 5 Bandwidth Boost for display traffic. VideoCardz points out an important caveat: Thunderbolt 5 still limits PCIe tunneling to 64 Gbps. That is roughly the bandwidth of four PCIe 4.0 lanes, while a desktop motherboard gives a graphics card a full x16 slot.
In practice, expect a high-end card in this dock to perform below the same card inside a desktop, with the gap depending on the game, the laptop and the connection. ASUS has not published performance numbers for the dock. Thunderbolt 4 laptops are supported too, but at lower connection speeds.
The graphics card's own video outputs remain available for your monitors as well.
ASUS's announcement does not give a price or a release date, and neither VideoCardz nor TechPowerUp reported one. The ROG XG Station 3 product page is live on the ROG website. Keep in mind that the dock is only part of the bill: you still need a graphics card and an SFX power supply, and high-end cards are hard to find right now. We recently covered the RTX 5090 supply situation .
An eGPU dock makes sense if you already own a recent Thunderbolt 5 laptop, carry it around, and want that same machine to become a desktop-class gaming or creative setup at your desk.
If you mostly play at home, a desktop is usually the simpler choice: the graphics card gets a full PCIe x16 link, the power supply and cooling are built in, and upgrades are straightforward. Our advice: wait for ASUS's price and independent reviews before buying the XG Station 3. If you want strong performance now, browse our gaming PCs , compare graphics cards , or look at our refurbished PCs for a lower-cost option.

Four oil tankers were destroyed after hitting naval mines in an area south of the Strait of Hormuz proscribed by Iran as prohibited for navigation, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday, as attacks on vessels in the region intensify while crude oil flows have dipped from recent highs.
The four tankers are still ablaze, while two other vessels have been seized, the Revolutionary Guards said.
While flows have recovered substantially from the lows in the spring, the security situation in and near the Strait of Hormuz has actually deteriorated, with a higher number of attacks on tankers in recent weeks.
Following a post-war peak in September, exports of crude oil, condensate, and fuels from the Middle East slipped to 17.1 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, down from 18.9 million bpd in September, according to data from Vortexa cited by Reuters .
“October data shows Middle East seaborne oil exports have pulled back slightly from recent post-war highs on heightened risks in the Strait of Hormuz,” George Morris, an analyst at Vortexa, said in comments reported by the publication.
Kpler has tracked a 1-million-bpd drop in total crude oil and condensate exports. Crude and condensate flows through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Gulf of Oman are estimated, provisionally, to have dropped to 16.1 million bpd in October, from 17.09 million bpd in September.
However, the tanker-tracking services caution that the numbers could be revised up as more details on shipments, especially shuttle shipments, emerge in the coming days.
Oil flows from the Middle East region have materially increased since the lows in April and May, but the heightened security concerns and intensified attacks, mines, and other explosions and incidents are making tracking shipments difficult. Tanker-trackers increasingly rely on satellite imagery to confirm movements because vessels are often switching off transponders to avoid detection when transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title_orig: Hackers use n-day exploits in zero-click attacks on iOS, Android devices
articles.title_zh: Hackers use n-day exploits in zero-click attacks on iOS, Android devices
articles.content_orig:
A large-scale watering hole attack associated with Russian hackers has been targeting iOS and Android users visiting compromised sites or fake ones impersonating legitimate portals.
The campaign used multiple high-profile websites in the U.S., Ukraine, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria that delivered the same payload for profiling visitors and their devices.
This initial stage allows the attacker to determine the browser version to deploy "platform-specific n-day exploit chains without user interaction."
Researchers at cybersecurity company Sekoia attribute the operation with moderate-to-high confidence to APT29 (aka Midnight Blizzard), a Russian threat group that was recently linked to hotel WiFi attacks .
Based on their findings, compromised legitimate sites belong to a Ukrainian gas producer, a U.S. chemical industry trade association, and a Bulgarian military-related site.
Lookalike domains impersonated the official America250 site and Raffles London at The OWO hotel, relaying content from the real sites in an adversary-in-the-middle attack model.
The researchers also discovered that the threat actor had compromised Ukrainian web analytics service Plerdy and modified its SEO tracker, which was loaded by thousands of websites, mostly in Ukraine, between August 27 and September 3.
In all cases, the initial payload was JavaScript code that profiled website visitors to determine their devices and browser versions. The command-and-control (C2) server then pushed the correct exploit chain.
According to Sekoia, the threat actors exploited the following vulnerabilities to extract cookies, messaging app databases, and credentials:
The researchers identified four other vulnerabilities in unreachable code or alternate exploit paths, but they were not used in the analyzed chains.
CVE-2025-43529 is linked to the “DarkSword” exploit kit , first documented in March, and leveraged in attacks since at least November 2025 by multiple threat groups.
Sekoia says that none of the payloads APT29 used in these attacks established persistence, allowing a device reboot to stop the malicious activity until visiting a compromised site again.
Regarding its attribution to APT29, Sekoia notes similarities to past watering-hole operations by the same threat group, infrastructure overlaps, and a compromised site that a partner linked to a 2025 APT29 campaign.
Apple and Google have patched all flaws targeted in this campaign, with fixes even reaching older iOS releases , so users are recommended to apply the latest available security updates for their devices.

articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields moved lower on Wednesday as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield was last seen 3 basis points lower at 4.9167%. The 30-year bond yield slid 3 basis points to 5.29%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield was broadly flat at 4.6101%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
Democrats are on course for a clean sweep, with the party winning at least the House and projected to win the Senate according to a CNBC Election Desk.
The Associated Press is projecting that Democrats have flipped Senate seats from Republicans in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Maine and Texas.
Stock futures fell sharply as election results rolled in. Contracts tied to the S&P 500 were seen 0.17% lower, and Nasdaq-100 futures slid 0.25%.
AI-related shares, which have led the bull market, paced the overnight decline on fears that Democrats would slow the data center buildout.

articles.title_orig: China calls for constructive ties with US amid Democratic gains in midterm elections
articles.title_zh: China calls for constructive ties with US amid Democratic gains in midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
The Democratic Party has regained control of the lower chamber of the United States Congress, winning the House of Representatives.
Late on Tuesday night local time, the House result was called in favour of the left-wing party.
Democrats needed to gain five seats to flip the chamber. Republicans have held a majority in the House since the 2022 midterms, during the presidency of Democrat Joe Biden.
The outgoing 119th House has 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies.
All 435 seats in the House were up for grabs in the election. A term in the House lasts only two years, compared with six for the Senate.
The Democrats’ victory in the House means their party leader in the chamber, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, will likely be selected as the speaker, the chamber’s top officer.
That position would make Jeffries the third in line for the US presidency, should the president and the vice president be removed from office.
He would also be the first Black person to serve in the role. He will replace outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana, who has held the post since 2023.
Democrats had been widely projected to regain control of the House, leveraging backlash to the second administration of President Donald Trump, which saw record-low approval ratings in the weeks leading up to the midterms.
For the last two years, Trump’s Republican Party has held a political “trifecta” in Washington, DC, with control of the presidency and both chambers of Congress. The 120th Congress is slated to be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
Democrats swept Republican-held House seats on their way to retaking the chamber.
In Iowa, Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott unseated Republican Zach Nunn in the state’s 3rd Congressional District.
In Virginia, Democrat Elaine Luria won a tight race against Republican incumbent Jen Kiggans, while in Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District, Democrat Janelle Stelson unseated seven-term Republican Scott Perry.
Meanwhile, Democrat incumbents Ilhan Omar and Ro Khanna sailed to victory, holding on to their seats in Minnesota and California.
Reacting to the Democratic wave, former President Barack Obama said the results showed voters wanted leaders who would bring people together and offer solutions to the problems they face.
“Tonight, the American people sent a clear message,” Obama wrote on X. He praised candidates who ran in areas long considered difficult for Democrats to win and urged supporters to keep organising during Trump’s remaining two years in office.
Senator Bernie Sanders said Democratic control of both chambers would allow the party to “hold Trump accountable”.
He urged Democrats to tackle income and wealth inequality. “We must aggressively fight for working families. No more excuses,” Sanders said.
Even Trump issued rare praise for the Democratic campaign in an interview with Fox News.
“I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard,” the president said.

articles.title_orig: Stocks, dollar slide as stunning victories for Democrats jolt AI bets
articles.title_zh: Stocks, dollar slide as stunning victories for Democrats jolt AI bets
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SINGAPORE, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Global stocks slumped and the dollar hit a one-month low on Wednesday as Democrats gained control of both the Senate and the House in the US midterm elections, fuelling fears that rapid AI sector growth could be hamstrung by regulatory scrutiny.
In ‌a major setback to President Donald Trump, Democrats notched up victories in the South Carolina, Texas and Ohio Senate races, capturing majorities in both the ‌Senate and House that reached deep into Republican strongholds.
The breadth of the party's success was underscored by gains in districts long considered safely conservative, highlighting a political shift that caught many investors off guard.
AI stocks ​were quick to slide. That in turn put the dollar under pressure, while cryptocurrencies also fell at the prospect of stronger regulations. Bonds, though, found favour as investors sought safer assets.
"Tighter regulatory scrutiny of technology and AI companies along with the higher likelihood of political gridlock beckon with a Democrat sweep," said Prashant Newnaha, senior rates strategist at TD Securities in Singapore.
The AI boom has helped propel global markets in recent years, driven by heavy spending from tech giants racing to build data centres and expand computing capacity. That has ‌left investors acutely sensitive to anything that could derail the ⁠technology's rapid expansion.
The election outcome could also hold broad implications for the US fiscal outlook as well as sectors such as defence, healthcare and banking.
S&P 500 futures were last down 0.35% while Nasdaq futures skidded more than 2% before cutting losses to trade down 0.5%. ⁠European futures were down 0.4%, having slid 1.5% earlier.
"Looks like investors are buying the dip after the initial knee-jerk selloff," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. "The blue sweep hasn't changed, but markets may be recognising that political gridlock doesn't necessarily mean weaker corporate earnings."
In Asia, the bulk of selling was in AI stocks, with chipmakers Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC sliding ​sharply ​before cutting losses. The KOSPI was last slightly higher after dropping 3% earlier.
George Efstathopoulos, portfolio manager ​and co-head of multi-asset research at Fidelity International, said he had ‌reduced overall equity exposure and dialled up exposure in defensive sectors like utilities, but thinks now is a good time to gradually rotate back into tech.
"The midterms are a clearing event that can allow investors to focus on sectors where fundamentals and pricing have diverged. Technology is one of them."
INVESTORS RUSH FOR SAFETY OF BONDS
Treasuries rallied as investors expect gridlock in Washington to cut government spending. AI regulation could also slow growth and reduce the need for rate hikes.
The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 6 basis points to 4.906%, pushing the dollar sharply lower. [FRX/] [US/]
"Bonds are coming out as the clear winner as markets put the AI trade on the chopping block ‌and embrace the higher possibility that further tax cuts are put on ice and government spending ​slows," said TD Securities' Newnaha.
Kim Seok-hwan, an analyst at Mirae Asset Securities, said the Democrats' victory in ​Texas is likely to weigh on chip stocks, raising fears of tighter ​curbs on AI data-centre development in one of the fastest-growing markets for computing infrastructure in the US.
"If Texas declares a moratorium on data ‌centres, as New York did, projects could face further delays," Kim ​said. "Today's market reaction is clearly reflecting concerns ​and uncertainty over these issues."
In currencies, the dollar slid broadly against major peers. The euro rose 0.5% to $1.1249, while sterling firmed 0.37% to $1.3464. That left the dollar index 0.37% lower at 101.34. [FRX/]
The yen and the Swiss franc — both safe-haven currencies — notched up the biggest gains. The yen was 0.7% stronger at 157.55 ​per US dollar, while the Swiss franc firmed almost 0.8% ‌to 0.8144 per US dollar.
In the oil market, prices were choppy on Wednesday after sliding to a four-week low in the previous session as ​investors weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran against worries that recent attacks in both conflicts could further disrupt supplies. [O/R]
(Reporting by ​Ankur Banerjee and Rae Wee in Singapore; Editing by Shri Navaratnam and Christopher Cushing)

articles.title_orig: US Equity Futures Inch Higher as Investors Await Midterm Results
articles.title_zh: US Equity Futures Inch Higher as Investors Await Midterm Results
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures were mixed early on Wednesday as traders speculated that Democrats were headed for majority control of Congress and some key gubernatorial wins in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections .
Futures tied to the S&P 500 traded 0.21% lower, while Nasdaq-100 futures shed 0.30%. But futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average moved higher, adding 29 points, or 0.06%. Futures were off their worst levels of the session.
The Democratic Party is projected to win both chambers of Congress, according to The Associated Press. The AP also projected that Texas Democratic governor candidate Gina Hinojosa is the winner over Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. Hinojosa has pledged a moratorium on data centers in the key tech hub.
Democrats securing a sizable majority in the House and Senate — the so-called blue wave scenario — would pressure the market and especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence buildout, according to some on Wall Street. Investors fear a big Democratic win could mean more restrictions on data centers nationwide. AI-linked stocks have already pulled back in recent weeks on concern about a slowing pace in data-center spending.
Big Tech shares Microsoft , Amazon and Nvidia were all trading lower in overnight trading on Robinhood.
Elon Musk's SpaceX was down 4.6% on Robinhood, while Tesla shares were down 4.1%. Data center play CoreWeave was down 3.2% in Robinhood overnight trading, while Alphabet was some 0.6% lower.
Equities "trended lower as it's looked more likely that Democrats are going to pick up the House and most likely the Senate," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, Tuesday evening as futures were pulling back.
He added: "If you get some governorships that are Democratic, what does that mean for the data center buildout, which has already seen a lot of skepticism over the last couple weeks in terms of the hyperscaler capex spending?"
AMD shares initially surged double digits in post-market action after the company, a key player in the AI trade, reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past analyst expectations. The stock was last 5% higher on Robinhood as stock market futures traded lower.
On the overall market, investors believe a blue wave would also be a headwind as it likely rules out any more business-friendly policies like tax breaks and possibly increases scrutiny on industries like banking.
Renewable shares like solar stocks traded higher in the post-market on speculation a Democratic majority in Congress would halt policies by President Donald Trump taken against the industry. The Invesco Solar ETF was up 3% in Robinhood trading.
President Donald Trump may have helped ease pressure on the market a bit overnight by not challenging the midterm results in an interview with the Wall Street Journal . Trump told the WSJ, "I think we'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them."
Treasury yields moved lower on Wednesday as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield was last seen 1 basis point lower at 4.9311%. The 30-year bond yield slipped 1 basis point to 5.3136%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield pulled back 1 basis point to 4.6017%.
European stock markets are set to open negative as investors respond to overnight projections of a major Democratic victory in the U.S. midterms.
The Democrats are projected to win both chambers of Congress, according to The Associated Press.
Stoxx 50 futures were lower by 0.35% ahead of Wednesday's market open.
Futures tied to the U.K.'s FTSE 100 were 0.64% lower, with Germany's DAX off by 0.46%. France's CAC 40 is set to start the session 0.28% lower, while Italy's FTSE MIB is down 0.21%.
Asian semiconductor stocks tumbled Wednesday as Democrats are projected to win both the House and the Senate in the U.S. midterm elections.
That has stoked worries over curbs on AI infrastructure buildout at a time when AI-linked stocks have been declining on concerns about weaker spending.
Japan's Softbank Group plunged over 8%, while chipmaking equipment company Disco fell 10.19%. Advantest shed over 8% and Renesas Electronics declined 7.64%. Tokyo Electron was down 7.04%.
South Korean chip heavyweights also came under pressure, with SK Hynix dropping 5.08% and Samsung Electronics declining 3.87%. Seoul Semiconductor shed 4.37%.
Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC slipped 1.09%.
Shares of Trump Media & Technology declined more than 7% in overnight trading on Robinhood as the 2026 midterm elections appear poised to conclude with a blue wave.
The stock moved lower after CNBC's Election Desk projected that Democrats are going to win the House. The party was also on track to take Senate control from Republicans.
President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post late Tuesday, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"
Japan's Nikkei 225 plunged more than 4% on Wednesday, leading losses across Asia-Pacific markets as renewed jitters over artificial intelligence stocks weighed on investor sentiment amid uncertainty surrounding the U.S. midterm elections.
The benchmark declined 4.45% to its lowest since May. Technology and energy stocks led declines in the benchmark, according to data from LSEG, while the broader Topix index tumbled more than 3%.
The sell-off came as investors weighed the prospect of tighter restrictions on data-center development under a potential Democratic-controlled Congress, adding to concerns over the outlook for AI-related spending.
Treasury yields fell as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield dropped nearly 5 basis points to 4.902%. The 30-year bond yield slid 5.29%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield pulled back 6 basis points to 4.55%. Read more .
Shares of SpaceX fell more than 6% on Robinhood overnight trading as Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa continued her lead over Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in the Texas gubernatorial race.
"Let's watch SpaceX. Let's watch Tesla . This is Elon Musk-land now. There are a lot of California companies that moved to Texas, thinking, 'All right, we're going to get out of this blue state and go somewhere safe,' and now it's proven that it isn't," Jay Woods, Freedom Capital Markets' chief market strategist, said in an interview with CNBC.
"You want to watch a lot of these Texas companies that moved there," he stressed.
Musk said that he was going to move the headquarters of both companies to Texas from California back in 2024. Tesla shares were down more than 4% on Robinhood.
Investors were focusing on the results of the Texas gubernatorial race for clues about the AI trade because the state represents an outsized portion of data center capacity. Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa has an early lead over Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. Hinojosa is calling for an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state and an end any tax incentives for the build-out.
"The one thing that could really end up moving stuff though would be if Abbott were to lose Texas," said Scott Ladner, chief investment officer of Horizon Investments. "Because there is a legitimate question about, where do you build these data centers?"
"Texas is a fertile ground for that. And if he were to lose, I think that fertile ground is largely barren. So, that's going to be a challenge. And so the AI trade — at least for next couple days — does hinge on does Abbott win or not," Ladner added.
Texas represents about 27% of U.S. data center gigawatts, estimates Wells Fargo.
— John Melloy and Sarah Min

Analysts are predicting an even worse third quarter for McDonald's home market. Wall Street is anticipating same-store sales declined 0.5%, according to StreetAccount estimates.
Investors will also be paying close attention to executive commentary about the fourth quarter so far. Chipotle Mexican Grill executives said last Wednesday that the restaurant industry saw traffic soften in October.
Shares of McDonald's have fallen about 11% over the last year, weighed down by investor concerns about its U.S. business, expensive plans to upgrade restaurants and the broader economy. The company has market cap of roughly $186 billion.

articles.title_orig: Chinese investors stay on sidelines despite Beijing’s latest rescue push
articles.title_zh: Chinese investors stay on sidelines despite Beijing’s latest rescue push
articles.content_orig:
Leveraged traders trimmed holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October
Chinese investors refrained from bets on stocks this week, even as state support unfolded after Beijing unveiled a litany of measures to shore up confidence in the world’s second-largest equity market.
Leveraged traders trimmed their holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October, according to official data. The retreat in retail enthusiasm contrasted with the government ramping up efforts to prop up stocks, including liquidity injections through two monetary tools and reported suspensions of new share sales to keep a lid on supply.
The divergence illustrates investors’ unease over whether the latest bout of government interventions will drive sustained gains in stocks, which are grappling with weak domestic demand and the fallout of a rout in AI stocks in the US. Investment banks including Bank of America and Macquarie said that state intervention might stabilise sentiment, but would fall short of fuelling a fresh rally.

articles.title_orig: Oil rises on Iran war uncertainty after Trump's Republicans face election rout
articles.title_zh: Oil rises on Iran war uncertainty after Trump's Republicans face election rout
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell Tuesday for a second consecutive session, as the market hopes the U.S. and Iran will reach a diplomatic settlement to the conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures lost 37 cents to close at $96.09 a barrel after dipping below $95 earlier in the session. Brent crude , the international benchmark, shed $1.17 to settle at $103.60.
The move lower came after rumors circulated the U.S. and Iran were making progress toward a deal.
Oil sold off more than 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran signaled they were both open to discussions to reach a settlement. President Donald Trump told reporters Tehran wants "to make a deal and that could happen."
Qatar is continuing to mediate talks between the U.S. and Iran, the Gulf state's foreign ministry said Tuesday. A delegation from Qatar held talks in Tehran in an effort to reach an agreement that prevents further escalation in the region and ends the U.S.-Iran conflict, the foreign ministry said.
However, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Emsaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion, according to the state-owned media outlet Islamic Republic News Agency . It was unclear where talks actual stand.
The market had been pricing in the risk of escalation after the U.S. midterm elections , as reports circulated that Washington was drafting plans for strikes on Iran. Crude prices gained more than 10% in October in response.
The situation in the Middle East remains volatile and there's still substantial risk that fighting could break out. Washington attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, adding that the U.S. has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks.
The military campaign against Iran has been kept deliberately low-profile to avoid signaling plans for a major escalation in fighting, the report said, quoting an unnamed official.
And commercial ships continue to come under attack in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman. At least four ship attacks have been reported since the start of the month, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
Despite these attacks, the Trump administration has also been touting a possible diplomatic solution to the conflict, with Vice President JD Vance telling CNN, "The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement."
On Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
High oil prices have contributed substantially to inflation and high gasoline prices in the U.S., which have become a cause of concern for Trump ahead of the midterm elections.
Last week, two Federal Reserve presidents said interest rates will need to move higher to rein in inflation. Higher rates generally crimp growth and raise costs for consumers, but help to bring down inflation.
— CNBC's Priyanka Salve contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Canva Announces Layoffs, Job Changes for About 22% of Workforce
articles.title_zh: Canva Announces Layoffs, Job Changes for About 22% of Workforce
articles.content_orig:
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.
The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.
It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.
The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.
"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."
The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.
Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.
Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.
"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.
The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.

articles.title_orig: Google researchers are fighting the company to tell the world what they know about AI
articles.title_zh: Google researchers are fighting the company to tell the world what they know about AI
articles.content_orig:
Workers inside Google’s artificial-intelligence division are asking executives to release them from non-disparagement agreements so they can discuss AI’s risks in public, The Washington Post reported. The request puts a plain question in front of one of the world’s most powerful AI employers: who gets to speak when the people closest to the technology think the public deserves a warning?
The reported dispute involves employees at Google DeepMind, including staff in London. A contract reviewed by The Washington Post reportedly bars some British employees from criticizing the company for life, including after they leave Google. Two current Google DeepMind workers told the paper that the agreements restrict public communication about AI’s potential impacts.
Google has pushed back on part of the picture. The company said it updated terms for new hires to remove the post-termination portion of non-disparagement clauses. A Google spokesperson added that the company does not enforce such clauses after employees leave and provides internal channels for escalating concerns. Disclosure pressure on AI labs is rising on several fronts, and our look at what the Anthropic amended S-1 disclosed on November 2 shows how much a lab now has to tell investors. This story asks the mirror-image question: how much can its workers tell everyone else?
Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
Four points hold up in the reporting available to us. First, workers in Google’s AI division are asking executives for release from non-disparagement agreements. Second, the dispute concerns Google DeepMind staff, including people based in London. Third, a contract The Washington Post reviewed reportedly bars some British employees from criticizing the company for life, even after they leave. Fourth, two current DeepMind workers said the agreements limit what they can say publicly about AI’s possible impacts.
Those are the load-bearing facts. Everything else around this story, including some of the headline phrasing that has circulated, goes further than the record does. The idea that Google researchers are collectively demanding the freedom to tell the world what they know about AI is a fair summary of the mood, but it is not independently established beyond the worker requests The Washington Post described. We have no verified count of participating researchers, no list of signatories, and no named organizer.
We also have no on-record quote from a named Google DeepMind researcher in the material available for this report. That matters for how much weight readers should put on any single claim. The two current workers appear in the reporting as sources describing the agreements, not as named spokespeople for a movement. A story built on a reviewed contract and two employees is still news, but it is a narrower story than a walkout or an open letter would be.
One detail deserves attention. The workers are reported to be asking executives to release them, which is a request, not a breach. That choice signals that at least some staff want to stay inside the rules while changing them. It also suggests they see the contract language, not company culture, as the obstacle.
A non-disparagement clause is a contract term that limits what a person can say publicly about their employer. Standard versions cover false or damaging statements. Broader versions can reach honest criticism, opinions, and even neutral descriptions of internal decisions if the wording is loose enough. Companies use them to protect reputation, and employees often sign them as part of an offer letter or a separation package without reading the fine print twice.
The difference between a narrow clause and a broad one is the whole story here. A narrow clause leaves room for a worker to say that a safety process failed or that a product carries a risk the public should weigh. A broad one makes the worker think twice before saying anything at all. When the subject is AI risk, a field where insiders often know things outsiders cannot check, that chilling effect carries real cost.
The reported contract goes beyond a standard employment-period restriction. According to The Washington Post, it bars some British employees from criticizing Google for life, including after they leave. A restriction that survives employment has no natural end date. A researcher who quits after five years of safety work would stay bound in year ten, even if the technology and the risks look nothing like they did at signing.
Note the qualifier in the reporting: the reviewed contract covers some British employees, not every DeepMind worker. We do not know the exact language used across the workforce, and the reporting does not claim a single uniform clause. Any reader judging Google’s conduct should keep that gap in view.
Google answered with two statements. The company said it updated terms for new hires to remove the post-termination portion of non-disparagement clauses. A spokesperson also said Google does not enforce non-disparagement clauses after employees leave, and that the company provides internal channels for people to escalate concerns.
Both statements carry weight, and both leave questions open. Removing the post-termination portion for new hires is a concrete contract change. It tells us Google’s lawyers saw enough risk or enough pressure to rewrite the template. A non-enforcement pledge is softer. It describes what the company does today, not what the paper allows tomorrow.
That distinction explains why employees are reported to be seeking clearer legal protection through revised contract language. A worker deciding whether to speak at a conference or give a journalist a background interview does not rely on a spokesperson’s description of enforcement habits. They rely on the text they signed. If the text says one thing and the practice says another, the safest move for the individual is silence.
Internal escalation channels address a different problem. They give employees a place to raise concerns inside the company, which helps when management listens. They do nothing for a worker who has raised concerns internally, seen no change, and now wants the public to know. The workers’ request, as reported, targets that second situation.
Google’s stated fix applies to new hires. The reporting we have does not say whether current employees, or people who already left under older terms, get the same change. That gap is the center of the dispute. A policy that improves the paperwork for the next cohort leaves the people who raised the issue on the old terms.
Several questions follow, and none has a confirmed answer in the available reporting:
Each question has a simple yes or no answer that Google could publish. The company’s decision on whether to answer them will say more about its posture than the original contract language did.
News about AI labs moves fast and headlines tend to outrun facts. The table below separates what the reporting supports from what it does not, so readers can see where the evidence stops.
Two lessons come out of that table. The core facts are solid because they rest on a document the paper reviewed and on company statements. The movement framing is softer, and readers should treat it as interpretation until someone names organizers or publishes a letter.
The reported contract covers British employees, and DeepMind has a major presence in London. That puts the dispute inside a country with its own regulators, its own employment rules, and its own public conversation about AI. UK officials have been vocal about AI risk in other domains. Our earlier report on the NCSC warning that AI malware could hit UK critical infrastructure within two years shows how seriously British security agencies treat the subject.
A government that asks the public to take AI risk seriously will find it awkward when the people who build the technology say they cannot

articles.title_zh: Midterm election results 2026: Who’s winning and what’s at stake for stocks and the economy
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Control of the US Congress is the prize on November 3, 2026, as Democrats attempt to wrest majorities from President Donald Trump's Republicans in the midterm elections.
Voters will also choose governors in 36 of the 50 states, and nearly every state will hold elections for its state-level legislative bodies.
Ballots have been cast for weeks, with early voting underway across the country ahead of Election Day .
The midterms , held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, by definition do not involve the president himself.
But anyone tempted to dismiss this year's contests as lacking drama or importance should weigh two statistics.
More than 100 million people are expected to cast ballots in this year's midterm voting, if turnout is anything like the previous midterm in 2022.
And as of October 30, a record $11.6 billion had been spent on political advertisements for the 2025–26 election cycle.
AdImpact, which tracks the activities, said the top spending is in battleground US Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Michigan.
Campaign finance records show Elon Musk alone has spent $442 million to support Republicans.
Midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races.
For example, more than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election.
In the House, Republicans currently hold a 218-214 majority, with two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans.
Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber.
The Senate is also in play, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority.
Democrats must net four additional seats to get control there.
Ten races, including those in Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia, could decide the outcome.
Trump's approval of his performance is at an all-time low of 32 percent, according to a September Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to affect the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.
Evidence suggests Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans.
If early voting trends continue, it could point to a Democratic win in November.
There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.
A landslide for the Democrats, however, is far from assured.
Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism toward Democrats, a Republican spending advantage in campaigns, and fears among moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.
Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress.
For 2026, that means Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.
The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.
Midterm election results can also give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.
Recent history shows the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.
In the 2010 midterms, during Barack Obama's Democratic presidency, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama's landmark healthcare reform legislation.
Democrats lost their majority.
In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.
The Republican wave was a "shellacking," Obama lamented at the time.
He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.
Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House.
They gained a net 40 House seats but lost a net two Senate seats.
At the state level, Republicans currently control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.
If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker — second in line for the presidency after the vice president — is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York.
He is currently the House Democratic leader.
Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to investigate a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates.
Jeffries has repeatedly said Democrats would look into what he has called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the Trump administration.
Jeffries also would steer Democrats' legislative priorities through the House.
He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable.
A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job.
Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill."
Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign.
An open seat in a Nebraska swing district, where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran, is also drawing attention.
Also high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.
Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.
Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted there is widespread cheating in US elections, despite a lack of evidence.
State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.
There is no set time for when the world will learn the results of the US midterm elections.
In tight races, winners may not be called for days or even weeks.
The first individual race calls are expected to start after polls begin to close in the United States on Tuesday night, first with Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. (ET) (2300 GMT).
Polls then close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia at 7 p.m. (0000 GMT on November 4).
The last polls to close are in far western Alaska at 1 a.m. ET.

articles.title_zh: Stock Market Election Night: Dow Futures, AI Stocks, Elon Musk In Focus; AMD, Arista Lead Earnings Winners (Live)
articles.content_orig:
Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jumping 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock was up 8% in extended trading.
Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter:
Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement . Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius rallied earlier Tuesday and remained higher after AMD reported results.
CEO Lisa Su said on the earnings call that she expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI growth to accelerate even faster than the company had projected 90 days ago. The company expects data center to drive the majority of its revenue and earnings growth.
"We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year," Su said on the earnings call.
AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But Intel's stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand .
The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago.
After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta 's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October.
"Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work," Su said on the earnings call with analysts.
AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI.
AMD is also a major player in the weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm -based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple.
Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research .
AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago.
For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount.
AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. Meta, Microsoft , Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering.
AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering .
During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." Su and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both made multiple trips to Taiwan and South Korea this year, holding meetings with key suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and memory leaders SK Hynix and Samsung.
In September, AMD said it would acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is developing a so-called world model that simulates 3D environments to aid in developing robots and other physically grounded AI applications.

articles.title_orig: Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
articles.title_zh: Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
articles.content_orig:
I’m getting some real mixed messages here, boys!
I’m getting some real mixed messages here, boys!
People, including on this staff, keep asking me with varying degrees of excitement or trepidation when the AI bubble will burst. I’ll tell you what I tell them: If I knew that, I would make a life-changing bet on the market, levered up as far as I could, and then, after I made my money, go retire on a beach somewhere. Maybe run a cat sanctuary, who knows.
What I can tell you is that I read with interest a story in Bloomberg this morning: “ Wall Street CEOs, Big Money Managers Divided Over AI Risks .” The story itself is a roundup of stuff said at the 2026 Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong. Here’s what caught my attention: The CEO of Pacific Investment Management Co. — that’s PIMCO, the legendary bond firm — told listeners that there’s going to be a downturn in the AI market “and then things are going to break.”
“What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.”
The astronomically expensive AI buildout has swamped debt markets — making it harder to raise cash. But there’s still more debt coming, and people still want to buy it. For instance, Meta drew $58 billion in orders for a bond offering that’s expected to be $15 billion to $20 billion, Bloomberg reported today. Oracle said Monday it would need another $20 billion in bonds , on top of its existing steep commitments . Alphabet, Google’s parent company, is selling €6 billion (or about $6.7 billion) of bonds. Even Microsoft recently sold bonds , for the first time in a decade — $25 billion of them.
The PIMCO CEO — his name is Emmanuel Roman, but his job is what matters here — has estimated that the AI buildout could create $2 trillion in financing needs over the next five years. The entire total US bond market is about $12 trillion.
I am harping on PIMCO because it has been instrumental in the AI trade. It was among the group of financiers that did the first CoreWeave chip-based financing in 2023. It made a quick $2 billion in paper gains from $29 billion in Meta bonds , meant to support the AI buildout, last year. It bought $4 billion of SpaceX bonds last month. If PIMCO’s CEO is publicly sounding the alarm about a bubble popping, that’s a big deal — especially since the company just sold a bunch of its AI debt .
It’s not just PIMCO urging caution. Apollo Global Management, which lately had been talking with SpaceX about a $40 billion chip deal , is also warning of AI risk. Apollo president Jim Zelter told analysts today that while he expects society will use “dramatically more computing power in the future” and that AI is improving quickly, there is still significant uncertainty. “What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.”
The sheer volume of interest on Meta’s bonds suggests we are not at the top of the market. But there have been reports from China that its AI bubble burst some time ago. Meanwhile Wall Street banks were tripping over themselves to finance $63 billion in debt from Anthropic — not even a hyperscaler.
This is what I mean when I say “I don’t know.” I do think, though, that something major — PIMCO’s Roman singled out US rate hikes, war, or a eurozone crisis as potential triggers — could flip this market. We’re not in go-go-go territory now. Maybe that will change; it’s possible Anthropic’s IPO will go blockbuster and it’ll be like when someone rolls up to a party that’s running low on beer with a 24-pack. But as more people are expressing caution — and particularly after the disaster at Situational Awareness — the best part of the party might be over.

articles.title_orig: Two helicopters collide near Mount Everest during rescue flight, killing one, injuring others
articles.title_zh: Two helicopters collide near Mount Everest during rescue flight, killing one, injuring others
articles.content_orig:
Video captures the moment two helicopters collide while trying to land at Pheriche Helipad in Nepal and the aftermath of the deadly accident.
Two helicopters collided while attempting to land just below Mount Everest base camp in Nepal.
The accident happened at about 8:12 a.m. Tuesday in the Pheriche area of Solukhumbu District, according to a translated press release from the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CAAN). The helicopters were identified as an Air Dynasty aircraft and a Fishtail Air aircraft, the aviation authority said.
Two foreign tourists were aboard the Fishtail Air helicopter. One of them, 47-year-old Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu of Chennai, India, died in the accident, according to CAAN.
DEADLY HELICOPTER CRASH KILLS 2 PILOTS BATTLING RAGING WILDFIRE IN YOSEMITE
The other tourist, New Zealand national Shailesh Kisan Patel, was injured, along with at least one pilot involved in the collision, the authority said.
Those injured in the collision were admitted to a hospital in Kathmandu for further treatment, according to the aviation authority.
The two helicopters pictured above collided while attempting to land just below Mount Everest base camp in Nepal. (Reuters)
CAAN has opened an investigation into the accident and will determine whether corrective action is needed based on its findings.
Fishtail Air said its helicopter crashed during landing while transporting passengers rescued from the Everest region , Reuters reported.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The Air Dynasty helicopter was carrying only cargo, an official with the company told Reuters.
Helicopters are a key form of transportation around Everest, where there are no roads. They are used to evacuate trekkers and guides suffering from illness or exhaustion amid the region's cold temperatures and high altitude, according to The Associated Press (AP).
The two helicopters shown above collided with each other while attempting to land near Mount Everest base camp in Nepal. (Viral Press)
Pheriche, where the accident occurred, sits about 13,780 feet above sea level and is located below Everest base camp, the AP reported.
The collision also came after heavy snow had covered trekking routes in the region.
Conditions improved Sunday, allowing thousands of trekkers to begin moving through the area again, according to the outlet.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Nepal has faced other major travel and safety challenges in recent months.
In September, about 70 Americans remained unaccounted for following catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border, while 18 Americans had been confirmed safe, Fox News Digital previously reported.
A damaged helicopter sits after two helicopters collided as they prepared to land in Nepal's Mount Everest region on Nov. 3, 2026. (Reuters)
The flooding was triggered by an Aug. 26 glacier collapse and caused widespread destruction, including flash floods and landslides. Rescue crews were searching areas, including hydropower project tunnels, where workers were believed to be trapped.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES
U.S. officials warned Americans at the time not to travel to the disaster zone because of the continued threat of additional flash floods and landslides.
At least 1,399 people across Nepal and China's Tibet region died in the disaster, with more than 5,400 others still missing at the time of the report.

Fox News' Gillian Turner, as well as Sophia Compton of Fox News Digital, contributed reporting.
Kelly McGreal is a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. She and the team cover travel, food and drink, health, relationships and more. She also produces the weekly American Culture Quiz and handles other special projects.

articles.title_orig: JetBlue Leads The Industry In Raising Checked Bag Fees… Again!
articles.title_zh: JetBlue Leads The Industry In Raising Checked Bag Fees… Again!
articles.content_orig:
For whatever reason, JetBlue tends to be the industry leader when it comes to raising checked bag fees, and competitors tend to follow. Earlier this year, JetBlue was the first major US carrier to raise checked bag fees , and now the airline is raising checked bag fees again…
Effective immediately (for tickets purchased as of November 3, 2026), JetBlue has increased checked bag fees . JetBlue has a rather complicated fee structure for checked bags, with both off-peak and peak pricing, plus different pricing based on whether you pay for the bag 24 hours or more in advance.
Below is a chart with JetBlue’s new checked bag fees.
As you can see, an off-peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $50-60 (depending on whether you pay in advance), while a peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $55-70 (depending on whether you pay in advance). For context, below are the dates that are considered peak for the purposes of bag fees.
It goes without saying that paying $50-70 for a first checked bag is a pretty substantial cost, especially when you consider how little checked bags used to cost. On a one-way, you’re looking at $100-140. For a family of four, you’d be looking at $400-560.
When JetBlue raised checked bag fees earlier this year, the airline released a statement claiming it was increasing checked bag fees to be “more competitive,” and that “while we recognize that fee increases are never ideal, we take careful consideration to ensure these changes are implemented only when necessary.” I imagine this time around, the logic is much of the same.
The simple reality is that oil prices are way up. Airlines have actually done a solid job of being able to make fare increases stick. But that’s not enough to fully offset the increase in the cost of jet fuel.
JetBlue is in a rough financial spot, and it hasn’t turned a profit since before the pandemic. The airline is hoping to turn an operating profit in 2027 , though that strikes me as being particularly optimistic. So the logic for raising checked bags is threefold:
JetBlue has just increased checked bag fees once again, and you’ll now pay $50-70 for a first checked bag on a domestic flight. This is JetBlue’s second price increase on checked bags so far this year. When airlines are trying to increase revenue, checked bag fees are often low hanging fruit.
When competitors match, it also becomes something that’s unavoidable for consumers, other than getting a credit card… which also has upside for the airline! I’d be shocked if other airlines don’t match this move from JetBlue.
What do you make of JetBlue increasing checked bag fees?

articles.title_orig: Hackers behind $6.3bn Binance heist ‘used malware and bogus job interviews’
articles.title_zh: Hackers behind $6.3bn Binance heist ‘used malware and bogus job interviews’
articles.content_orig:
Binance released on Tuesday a detailed investigation into the $6 billion hack of its cryptocurrency platform, showing how attackers used fake job interviews and malicious code to steal the funds.
The crypto exchange said it had replenished 98 percent of the affected assets by drawing on its own funds, with the remaining amount involving little-traded currencies that are harder to acquire.
The attack, carried out over about four hours on October 29, was attributed by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to North Korea-affiliated hackers.
Pyongyang has denied the allegations, with the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un calling the claim "absurd rhetoric."
Around $2.85 billion of the stolen $6.34 billion has been frozen, Binance said, meaning that the attackers could not use it or convert it to another currency.
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply.
According to Binance, attackers took their first steps towards the breach as early as June.
First, they targeted a platform engineer by getting them to download a virus-laden version of the widely-known programming software Homebrew.
Binance's cybersecurity teams identified the malware and removed it, but the hackers had already had time to harvest information about the engineer and his colleagues.
In September, the attackers approached another Binance engineer through a legitimate job-search platform, offering him an interview for a position in a fictitious company.
After building trust with the subject through the sharing of social media photos and videos, they asked the engineer to download a test exercise as part of the interview process.
The exercise contained malware that deployed "sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques," Binance said, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version.
That malware was critical to the success of the attack, as it allowed the hackers to establish a connection with Binance's internal systems.
On October 20, the attackers used the access they had gained and an internal AI tool to gain control over software used by two other engineers.
Nine days later, they triggered malicious code that initiated the attack.

articles.title_orig: China seeks APEC solutions to world development ahead of leaders’ summit
articles.title_zh: China seeks APEC solutions to world development ahead of leaders’ summit
articles.content_orig:
China on Tuesday urged Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) members to continue contributing practical and effective "Asia-Pacific solutions" to the region's and the world's development, according to media reports.
Top diplomat Wang Yi highlighted the importance of the upcoming APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting later this month in an address to the 37th Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Ministerial Meeting via video conference, state-run Xinhua News reported.
Wang, who co-chaired the meeting with Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, said Beijing is willing to work with "all parties" to do a "good job" in the final stage of the 2026 APEC "China Year" and contribute to the fruitful results at the leaders' meeting.
He said the leaders' meeting is an "important one" concerning the future development of the Asia-Pacific region.
The commerce minister urged all APEC parties to uphold free trade and innovation-driven development, foster a vibrant engine for growth, advance discussions and policy coordination on digital and intelligent economic and trade rules, and build a fair and equitable international economic and trade order.
China will host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen in south China in November. It will mark the country's third time hosting the event, following Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014.
The theme of the summit is "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together.” China has identified openness, innovation and cooperation as the three priority areas for this year's APEC cooperation.

articles.title_orig: What the midterm elections could mean for markets, debt
articles.title_zh: What the midterm elections could mean for markets, debt
articles.content_orig:
‘Varney & Co.’ host Stuart Varney examines a potential socialist surge, Republican upsets in red states and what an election shakeup could mean for Congress and Wall Street.
Voters across America are casting their ballots in the midterm elections on Tuesday, which will determine control of Congress and could add to investors' concerns about oversight of the artificial intelligence (AI) sector and how the debt ceiling will be addressed next year.
Since President Donald Trump's second term began in 2025 with Republican majorities in both chambers of Congress, the S&P 500 has gained about 27% in part due to a massive influx of spending on AI and strong earnings growth.
Treasury yields are also significantly higher in part because of geopolitical risks that emerged with the outbreak of the Iran war in late February, which caused a surge in energy prices. U.S. budget deficits have continued to widen to about $2 trillion, adding more upward pressure to yields as debt issuance mounts.
Investors are weighing how the results of the election will affect the outlook for financial markets depending on whether Democrats take control of one or both chambers of Congress.
AFFORDABILITY TAKES CENTER STAGE AS AMERICANS CAST THEIR BALLOTS IN HIGH-STAKES MIDTERMS
The midterm elections will determine control of Congress for the next two years, carrying implications for the nation's finances and markets. (J. David Ake/Getty Images)
Since 1930, there have been eight midterm cycles when the president's party lost control of the House, and the S&P 500 rose for the remainder of the year five times, Ned Davis Research said. It posted a median gain of 1.4% from Election Day through year-end, slightly less than the 1.9% posted across all post-Election Day midterm years.
In a scenario in which Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress , investors expect tougher oversight of AI which could weigh on markets that have been pushed higher by the emerging tech.
Democratic majorities would have the ability to investigate corporate America while attempting to slow deregulation , which could increase market volatility.
DSA PLATFORM COULD COST UP TO $212T OVER A DECADE, ANALYSIS FINDS
Markets have generally fared well under divided government. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
If Democrats win the House but Republicans hold their majority in the Senate, implications for the U.S. fiscal situation could be mixed.
Bipartisan compromises would be required over issues like funding the government to avoid shutdowns and raising the debt ceiling , which could create the potential for brinkmanship.
In a scenario where Republicans retain their majorities in the House and Senate, the GOP could pursue further tax reforms or boost defense spending.
FEDERAL BUDGET DEFICIT HITS $2T AS NATIONAL DEBT COSTS SURGE
The results of the midterms will impact negotiations between Congress and the Trump administration depending on who controls the House and Senate. (Grant Baldwin/AFP via Getty Images)
Ned Davis chief U.S. strategist Ed Clissold said that a House takeover by Democrats could modestly temper the U.S. equity market's year-end rally, but in general it hasn't prevented stocks from advancing.
"Conventional wisdom is that gridlock is good (for stocks)," said Clissold, adding that stocks have performed better under Democratic presidents than Republicans.
Diego Barnuevo, market analyst at Ebury, said that a Democratic-held Congress' negotiations with the White House would likely be limited to the budget and debt ceiling, and that a "Democratic sweep would be neutral to mildly positive for the fiscal outlook."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A Republican sweep could ease concerns over investigations into AI companies that carry the potential to rattle markets.
"If Republicans maintain control of Congress, that would likely provide the most supportive incremental federal policy backdrop for the AI/infrastructure buildout through policy continuity, potential fiscal expansion, deregulation and faster federal permitting," JPMorgan strategists said in a note.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Google to shut off search for schools that opt out of AI
articles.title_zh: Google to shut off search for schools that opt out of AI
articles.content_orig:
Google announced Tuesday morning that it would switch off AI products by default for students in schools that use the technology giant’s education software. But those schools that forgo its AI services would also be cut off from Google Search.
The move comes after mounting criticism from advocacy groups and senators about the spread of Google’s AI services available in classrooms. Until Tuesday, its AI products — branded under the Gemini moniker — were automatically activated for schools using Google Classroom.
Google said Tuesday’s move would also cut off students’ access to Google Search if schools do not enable Gemini, given AI’s growing integration into the company’s search products.
Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post announcing the change that access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search “will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.”
“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Phillips wrote.
Some education and technology advocates immediately slammed the decision, painting the move as a punishment for schools that don’t use Google’s AI. “It is unfortunate that Google has prioritized its business interests over the education of our children,” said Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, a national educators union.
“Instead of working with teachers and parents to uphold privacy and ensure their tools are safe and useful, it throws the baby out with the bathwater and bans access to the tools altogether,” she told NBC News in written comments.
Josh Golin, executive director of advocacy group Fairplay, said in a statement that Google is attempting “to strong-arm schools into using its AI products.”
“Schools should use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click,” Golin said.
In a statement posted to social media after this article was published, Google said the announcements “give schools more choice, not less,” and that schools can turn on Google Search individually without enabling Gemini products. But Search will still have AI features built into it, which the company said have been updated “to make it better for learning. Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork.”
Earlier this year, Google turned on Gemini in its Classroom app, allowing children — regardless of age — to access AI products unless districts disabled it .
Parent advocacy groups and experts on the use of technology in schools denounced Google for providing AI products to children — raising concern that students would outsource their work to AI systems on school devices — and lobbied school districts to disable Gemini products. In an open letter in early October, 13 leading parent advocacy organizations — including the Digital Childhood Institute and Schools Beyond Screens — called on school districts to turn off access to Gemini and YouTube, which is also owned by Google .
Google has established a dominant role in education technology over the past 15 years. The vast majority of Chromebook laptops are purchased by school districts to provide to students. Nearly two-thirds of assignments use a Google product, according to a 2023 report by the firm Schoolytics. This year, the company began offering multiday AI trainings for educators, featuring sessions that focused on how they could mitigate pushback by teachers who don’t want to use AI.
Research on AI in educational settings has not established a long-term benefit for students. There are no high-quality causal studies into student use of AI, according to the SCALE Initiative at the Stanford Graduate School of Education . Researchers have also warned that many of the studies conducted so far on AI in education didn’t measure whether it boosted learning and often did not test whether AI-assisted learning was superior to other teaching methods.
In Tuesday’s blog post , Google said that for schools that enable the company’s AI products, they will now detect when a student is trying to use them just to get an answer on an assignment. A redesigned version of Google Search will instead walk students through the topic or problem and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer, the company said.
Jared Perlo is a technology reporter focused on AI for NBC News Digital.
Tyler Kingkade is a national reporter for NBC News, based in Los Angeles.
